items.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
items.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

items.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
items.summary: The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
items.body:
Europe

French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault

November 27, 20266:49 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Actor Gerard Depardieu arrives to face trial for the alleged sexual assaults of two women on a film set in 2021, on March 24, 2025 in Paris.

Aurelien Morissard/AP

hide caption

Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.

Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.

The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.

The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.

A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.

"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").

The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.

Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate

The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."

The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.

In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.

His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

法国影星热拉尔·德帕迪约因强奸和性侵指控被勒令受审

2026年11月27日 上午6:49（美国东部时间）

作者

美联社

资料图——2025年3月24日，演员热拉尔·德帕迪约抵达巴黎，就2021年片场两名女性遭性侵的指控出庭受审。

奥雷利安·莫里萨尔/美联社

隐藏图注

奥雷利安·莫里萨尔/美联社

巴黎——当局周四表示，数十年来法国最负盛名的演员之一热拉尔·德帕迪约已被勒令就强奸和性侵一名年轻女演员的指控接受审判。此时距这位影星在另一起案件中放弃对性侵定罪判决的上诉不到两周。

女演员夏洛特·阿尔努尔2018年指控德帕迪约在其巴黎家中强奸她，当时她22岁。

八年后，巴黎上诉法院裁定，这位演员应就2018年8月7日强奸和性侵的指控接受审判，同时驳回了与六天后第二起事件相关的指控。

现年77岁的德帕迪约否认了强奸指控。他的律师德尔菲娜·梅耶告诉美联社，他对周四的裁决提出异议，但未说明是否会向法国最高民事和刑事法院提出挑战。

该裁决维持了调查法官2025年8月将德帕迪约送交审判的裁定的一部分。

此案已成为法国反思性暴力问题中最受关注的案件之一，因为#MeToo运动在该国遭遇阻力，尤其是在艺术界。

一位法国电影偶像面临#MeToo的清算

德帕迪约身材魁梧、鼻梁歪斜、银幕气场强大，统治法国影坛半个世纪。

他成为法国最知名的文化输出之一，凭《大鼻子情圣》获奥斯卡提名，凭《绿卡》获金球奖。

但性行为不当的指控及其随后的定罪，日益盖过他的电影成就。

11月16日，德帕迪约放弃对2021年片场性侵两名女性定罪判决的上诉，接受18个月缓刑，并公开道歉，这与他此前在该案中的否认态度截然不同。

“因此，我向那些可能受到伤害的人致以深切而真诚的歉意，”他在一份书面声明中说。

德帕迪约于2025年5月被判在拍摄《绿色百叶窗》期间猥亵一名布景师和一名助理罪名成立。

法院还下令将其姓名列入法国全国性犯罪者数据库。

“在片场，我长期以来一直躲在挑衅和粗俗幽默背后。我以为我的言语和一些行为没有后果。但事实并非如此，尤其是出自一个曾拥有我那样权力的人，”德帕迪约说。

对德帕迪约的指控引发全国辩论

2023年12月，一部电视纪录片显示他在2018年朝鲜之行期间多次发表淫秽言论并做出淫秽手势，围绕德帕迪约的争议随之加剧。

就连法国总统埃马纽埃尔·马克龙也介入其中，称这位演员“让法国骄傲”，招致女权活动人士的批评。马克龙援引无罪推定原则，并表示他不会参与“猎巫”。

这场争议暴露了该国的分歧，一些知名文化人物曾抵制#MeToo运动。

2018年，女演员凯瑟琳·德纳芙和其他99名女性签署公开信，捍卫男性向女性示好的自由，并警告她们所认为的运动过激行为。

德帕迪约1948年出生于法国中部城市沙托鲁的一个工人阶级家庭，克服语言障碍，成为法国最多产的演员之一。他的职业生涯横跨数百部电影，从《最后一班地铁》和《恋恋山城》到广受欢迎的《阿斯泰利克斯》系列。

他在银幕外的放纵行为也登上国际头条，尤其是2013年因法国税收纠纷接受俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京颁发的俄罗斯护照。

Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform

Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms.

FILE PHOTO: The Pentagon is seen from the air in Washington, U.S., March 3, 2022. REUTERS/Joshua Roberts/File Photo

WASHINGTON: Hackers have breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardise a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities".

A ONE-STOP SHOP

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators - Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet - to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world.

SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.

Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.

"A breach here is a big deal," one of the sources said.

Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.

Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

A RANGE OF DISRUPTION

The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.

All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.

Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.

STRING OF HACKS

News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.

Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.

In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One's leadership touted what they called a "100 per cent success rate" in beating back what they said was a "staggering" number of attempts to penetrate the platform.

"There is no room for error when it comes to security," Cloud One's leadership wrote.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities".
A ONE-STOP SHOP

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators - Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet - to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world.

Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.

Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.
Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.

AMSTERDAM: Dutch authorities seized 26 critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles at Schiphol airport last week, the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday (Nov 27).

The Vallarta turtles, one of the world's smallest turtle species, were brought in from Mexico, where only around 300 of them remain in the wild.

They were hidden in the checked baggage of a man who was travelling to Hong Kong, the NVWA said. The man was arrested and further investigations are ongoing.

Wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving, most of the turtles were packed in a box together with a toy car, while a few others were placed inside a sealed sock.

NVWA said they all survived and were taken to a specialist animal rescue centre.

Vallarta mud turtles can sell for up to US$30,000 each, the US-based Center for Biological Diversity said last month in a statement calling on the Mexican government to do more to protect the animals.

items.summary: The measure is the first such operation since the Cold War and comes amid fears of Russian aggression in Europe.

Around 100,000 British defence veterans contacted amid ‘heightened threat’

The measure is the first such operation since the Cold War and comes amid fears of Russian aggression in Europe.

LONDON: Britain’s armed forces have contacted around 100,000 veterans to strengthen “preparedness and deterrence” as British defence minister Wes Streeting on Thursday (Nov 26) evoked a heightened threat environment.

The precautionary measure is the first such operation since the Cold War and concerns around 100,000 former military personnel who make up the strategic reserve, media reports said.

The move comes amid fears of Russian aggression in Europe following Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Under the terms of their service, some former armed forces members are “liable to return to military service in exceptional circumstances, including a national emergency or a transition to war”, a British Ministry of Defence statement said.

The veterans of the British Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force were being contacted to ensure their details were up to date and included any skills they acquired since leaving.

The reservists could volunteer for training and exercises such as NATO’s flagship Steadfast Defender next spring.

'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' says Germany's Merz as he defends aid for Kyiv

Streeting said gathering such information should be standard and people should be reassured rather than alarmed by it.

“There’s no doubt, and I’ve talked about this as have all of my counterparts across NATO in recent days, weeks, and months, we are operating in a heightened threat environment, and so this degree of readiness, I think, is a sensible, necessary precaution,” he told Sky News.

Thousands of British and French troops in October took part in a military training exercise designed for defending NATO countries against a modern-day attack.

“These letters do not mean reserves are about to be mobilised,” said Veterans Minister Calvin Bailey.

He described the initiative as “simply good housekeeping to make sure we know how to contact those who are eligible and keep up to date on their skills and experience”.

Last month, the British government advised the public to keep at least three days of emergency supplies at home, a message it said had been hammered home by ‌the recent PHP software glitch, as well as a record-setting summer of heat, drought and wildfires.

Flaws in the PHP programming language had been disclosed, prompting governments and businesses worldwide to rush to secure their systems, forcing ​some services offline and triggering millions of hacking attempts in ⁠one of the most significant cybersecurity incidents in recent years.

The ​British government said the internet outage showed the importance of its ​newly launched Be Ready campaign, which advises the public to keep three days of bottled water and non-perishable food in the house.

items.title: Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson files High Court appeal bid
items.summary: Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her three elderly in-laws by feeding them beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms.
items.body:

World

Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson files High Court appeal bid

Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her three elderly in-laws by feeding them beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms.

Erin Patterson is escorted out of the Supreme Court of Victoria in Melbourne on Aug 25, 2025. (File photo: AFP/Martin Keep)

Read a summary of this article on FAST.

Get bite-sized news via a new
cards interface. Give it a try.

Click here to return to FAST
Tap here to return to FAST

FAST

SYDNEY: An Australian woman convicted of murdering three of her estranged husband's relatives with a meal laced with deadly mushrooms on Friday (Nov 27) filed an appeal bid with Australia's top court.

Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her three elderly in-laws by feeding them beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms, in a case that gripped Australia.

Last month, the Court of Appeal in the Supreme Court of Victoria rejected Patterson's attempt to quash her conviction. The High Court is her last opportunity to appeal her conviction.

Patterson has consistently maintained her innocence, saying the deaths were an accident.

Patterson's application to the High Court rests on some of the same grounds as her Supreme Court action, according to court documents.

A general view of Erin Patterson’s house in Leongatha, Australia, on Jun 24, 2025. (Photo: Reuters/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

"The Court of Appeal erred in its application of principles that justice must not only be done, but be seen to be done," said Patterson's appeal bid, filed by her lawyers on Friday.

The grounds include arguments that some evidence should have been excluded from the trial and that the jury's accidental accommodation in the same hotel as other people involved in the case undermined the verdict.

Patterson initially received a life sentence with a minimum of 33 years before being eligible for parole, but the prosecution appealed, arguing that it was inadequate in light of the seriousness of the crimes.

Victoria's Supreme Court last month upheld the prosecution's appeal and sentenced Patterson to life without parole — only the second time in Australian history such a sentence has been handed down to a woman.

A jury last year found Patterson invited her mother-in-law Gail Patterson, father-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, to a 2023 lunch at her home in Leongatha, a town of about 6,000 people, some 135km southeast of Melbourne, and fed them the poisoned lunch.

She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather’s husband, who survived the meal.

The 11-week trial, held in the nearby country town of Morwell, attracted worldwide attention, and the case has since spawned several podcasts and books.

Source: Reuters/lk

items.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
items.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

ByGeeta Pandey

Women & Social Affairs Editor, India

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.

More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed

South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

• In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage

• Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict

• India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.

Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries

"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."

The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

• India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it

• India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.

"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."

Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.

File photo. Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araqchi, attends a press conference during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), at UN headquarters in New York City, US, Sep 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Bing Guan)

SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke by telephone on Thursday (Nov 26) with South Korea's Cho Hyun, who reaffirmed Seoul did not intend to join any war or deploy troops to the Gulf, the Iranian embassy in Seoul said in an X post on Friday.

South Korea's parliament is reviewing a government motion to broaden the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to include the outer waters of the Gulf of Oman to help ensure safe navigation of its commercial vessels.

The anti-piracy Cheonghae unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009.

Araqchi said the presence of foreign militaries "would instead heighten tensions and expand the scope of conflict", the Iranian embassy said.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry said Cho explained that the mission of the navy unit was to ensure the safety of South Koreans and protect the country's economic interests.

South Korea, which is one of the world's largest oil and gas importers, sourced 70 per cent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, with most shipments delivered through the Strait of Hormuz, according to government data.

items.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
items.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
items.body:
Obituaries

Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died

November 27, 20261:12 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008.

Franka Bruns/AP

hide caption

Franka Bruns/AP

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.

FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993.

James Finley/AP

hide caption

James Finley/AP

Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."

Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.

Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.

He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.

His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

讣告

前《时代》杂志记者、副国务卿斯特罗布·塔尔博特去世

2026年11月27日 凌晨1:12（美国东部时间）

作者

美联社

资料图——2008年7月16日，布鲁金斯学会主席斯特罗布·塔尔博特在柏林出席一场新闻发布会时发言。

Franka Bruns/美联社

隐藏图注

Franka Bruns/美联社

斯特罗布·塔尔博特，曾任《时代》杂志记者，后于比尔·克林顿总统任内担任副国务卿，之后又执掌布鲁金斯学会，于周四去世，享年80岁。

其子德文·塔尔博特证实，他在纽约州东汉普顿的家中久病之后安详离世。

老塔尔博特曾就读于耶鲁大学和牛津大学，在牛津期间与克林顿同住。在英国求学时，他曾在《时代》杂志莫斯科分社实习，随后该杂志请她协助翻译尼基塔·赫鲁晓夫泄露的回忆录。赫鲁晓夫是苏联共产党前第一书记，于1964年被赶下台。

资料图——1993年1月2日，当选总统比尔·克林顿与《时代》杂志的斯特罗布·塔尔博特在南卡罗来纳州希尔顿黑德岛的海滩上散步时私下交谈。

James Finley/美联社

隐藏图注

James Finley/美联社

塔尔博特完成了这项工作，这让他年纪轻轻便小有名气，并因此获得了该杂志的一份工作。

据美国国务院为其撰写的传记，他在《时代》杂志工作了21年，主要关注苏美关系，曾任华盛顿分社社长和外交事务专栏作家。此后，他接到了刚刚当选的克林顿的电话。

塔尔博特于1994年加入美国国务院，很快升任副国务卿。在这一职位上，他是克林顿政府对俄及其他前苏联国家政策的制定者，并在1998年印度核试验后主持了美印之间的谈判。

“斯特罗布是一位善良而杰出的人，他让我们的世界更加和平与安全，”克林顿在塔尔博特去世后发表的一份声明中说。他说，塔尔博特在牛津翻译赫鲁晓夫回忆录时，每天为他做早餐是克林顿的任务，并补充道：“不知怎的，我占了便宜。”

他说，他和希拉里都对“一位了不起的朋友、一位世界级人物的离去”“深感悲痛”。

此后，他于2002年至2017年担任布鲁金斯学会主席。在此期间，他还主持了美国国务院外交事务政策委员会。

塔尔博特还著有十余本书。他的最后一本书名为《我们国父的警告：理性时代遇上特朗普时代》，于2020年出版。

他1946年出生于俄亥俄州代顿，身后留下两个儿子德文和阿德里安，以及六个孙辈。

他的第一任妻子布鲁克·希勒于2009年去世，他后来与作家芭芭拉·拉齐尔·阿舍结婚。

items.summary: If Prime Minister Christopher Luxon cannot reach a deal to form a ruling coalition, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

New Zealand’s ruling coalition falls just short of majority in final election count

If Prime Minister Christopher Luxon cannot reach a deal to form a ruling coalition, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

People enter a voting place at St Anne’s Anglican Church on the day of the general election in Wellington, New Zealand, Nov 7, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Hollie Adams)

WELLINGTON: New Zealand’s ruling centre-right coalition has narrowly missed winning a parliamentary majority, final election results showed on Friday (Nov 27), leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon needing the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power.

If Luxon cannot reach either a coalition or confidence-and-supply deal, and any negotiations between other parties fail to produce a majority government, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

Electoral Commission results showed the coalition with 65 seats, one seat short of a majority in the 130-seat parliament.

"New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term," Luxon told a news conference.

"Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls."

OPPORTUNITY TO NEGOTIATE WITH NATIONAL

Luxon’s centre-right National Party secured 40 seats in the Nov 7 election, and its junior coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.

Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats.

New entrant to parliament Opportunity won seven seats, and its leader Qiulae Wong said on Friday she would negotiate with National as the party with the largest number of seats.

"I don't think anybody can rule anything out at this stage because we haven't had any discussions," Wong told a press conference, adding all options were on the table including being on the crossbenches.

New Zealand poised for weeks of political wrangling after knife-edge poll

New Zealand’s centrist kingmaker says populism failing voters worldwide

"We are going to do everything we can to make sure that there is a stable government," she said.

Opportunity's platform includes stronger climate commitments, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, tighter competition rules and a more interventionist approach to public investment, policies that cut against parts of the coalition's agenda.

ACT Party leader David Seymour said government formation could happen "quite rapidly" if the parties involved worked together to come to an agreement.

"The government can be formed if the coalition is prepared to work with Opportunity at some level," he said in an interview with 1News.

The results show a centre-left coalition of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori would not be able to form a government, even with the support of Opportunity.

However, if NZ First were to strike a deal with the centre-left parties — as it did with Labour after the 2017 election — they could form a coalition government.

The New Zealand dollar, which hit a 17-year low against the US dollar this week, strengthened slightly after the announcement of the election results.

Earlier this month, preliminary results from the Electoral Commission had shown the ruling coalition with a majority of two seats. The final tally includes special votes, which include those from people voting overseas or outside their electorate, and typically skew left.

The Electoral Commission said there were 2,931,604 votes cast, of which 484,865 were special votes.

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday (Nov 26) that he had seen sufficient information that Nvidia's Jensen Huang was not a security threat, while touting his administration's intervention to save the scandal-plagued CEO's job as "a great thing" for the world.

"I think he's absolutely fine," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate.

Asked by AFP how he could be sure when the Justice Department would not confirm it had conducted a thorough investigation into Huang, Trump said his belief was based on "information I have, which is a lot of information".

Huang, a key figure in the AI revolution, was forced to resign earlier this month after revelations that he had an affair with a business executive who reportedly has ties to Chinese intelligence and whose company may have helped China obtain advanced chips in violation of US export controls.

Trump revealed that he and other officials in his administration have worked behind the scenes to push for Huang to be reinstated, in a highly unusual intervention by the government into a top company's decision making.

"So I really ... think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world," Trump said of the effort to back Huang.

Asked if he had spoken with Huang since his reinstatement was announced, Trump said no, but then later said: "When I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term."

items.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
items.summary: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
items.body:
World

Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate

November 26, 20268:47 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

hide caption

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

BUNIA, Congo (AP) — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

items.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
items.summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
items.body:
World

North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture

November 26, 20268:31 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026.

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

hide caption

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

translation.summary: 据报道，金正恩领导人视察了生产核原料的设施，并呼吁制造更多核武器，以应对来自美国和韩国的威胁。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
translation.body:
世界

朝鲜金正恩无视特朗普的会面提议后誓言建造更多核武器

2026年11月26日 上午8:31 东部时间

作者

美联社

在这张朝鲜政府提供的照片中，领导人金正恩于2026年11月25日星期一在朝鲜一处未公开地点视察政府所称用于生产武器级核材料的设施。

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

隐藏图注

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

韩国首尔（美联社）——朝鲜领导人金正恩视察了生产核原料的设施，并呼吁建造更多核武器。几天前，他无视了美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在最近访问亚洲期间提出的会面提议。

专家表示，金正恩很可能想展示其不断发展的核武库——这是他威权统治的支柱——并重申他拒绝未来就拆除其核计划进行任何谈判。

朝鲜官方媒体朝鲜中央通讯社周四表示，金正恩视察了两家核材料生产工厂，其中一家新近落成，另一家正在扩建。朝中社照片显示，金正恩和高级军事官员走在密集排列的、看似用于生产武器级铀的离心机之间，并参观了展示据信为弹头的展厅。部分图像被模糊处理。

朝中社称，金正恩周三还视察了一个核动力设备生产基地和一个核研究所。

自2010年向到访的美国学者展示其主要宁边核综合设施的一处铀浓缩设施以来，朝鲜已数次公开铀浓缩设施。朝鲜没有说明金正恩本周视察的核材料生产工厂位于何处。今年6月，朝鲜在报道金正恩视察时公开了一处铀浓缩设施的部分内容，外部专家评估那很可能是宁边的一处额外铀浓缩设施。

金正恩以美国和韩国的威胁为由为核计划辩护。金正恩表示，他最近的视察是其加强朝鲜防御能力努力的一部分，以应对“时刻逼近朝鲜半岛的变幻莫测的核威胁”。据朝中社报道，他指责美国煽动其地区盟友拥有核动力潜艇，并承诺与其分享核武器。

据朝中社报道，金正恩说：“我们拥有核武器的正当性和实质性，以及我们在质量和数量上加强核能力的趋势，是不可逆转的现实。”

金正恩还表示，鉴于朝鲜“面临与最危险敌对国家接壤的不可避免的现实”——指的是韩国——在多个领域部署用于各种任务的低当量战场核武器至关重要且紧迫。近年来，随着与韩国敌意加剧，朝鲜一直专注于发展此类战术核武器。

“特朗普谈到了愿意与金正恩会面，但美国要求朝鲜无核化的基本立场没有改变。所以金正恩想说‘看看我们有多强大。如果想见我们，就别谈无核化’，”首尔韩国国家战略研究院分析师文成默说。

文成默表示，金正恩视察核设施也可能意在检查国家核计划目标今年取得了哪些进展，以及在年底劳动党会议之前必须设定哪些未来目标。

韩国国防部表示，韩方严肃对待金正恩关于战场核武器的言论，并补充说，首尔在韩美同盟下对平壤的核威胁保持坚定的军事戒备。韩国联合参谋本部拒绝分享对朝中社报道的朝鲜核设施的分析，称这是韩国和美国的机密信息。

特朗普仍希望与金正恩会面。特朗普上周访问中国出席亚太经济合作组织峰会时重申了他恢复与金正恩外交的渴望。但特朗普与金正恩的会面并未发生，平壤没有公开回应特朗普的提议。

本周在接受《纽约邮报》采访时，特朗普驳斥了金正恩拒绝其示好的说法，称：“不，他没有无视。你知道，我们在那里有很多领导人……总会有我们见面的时候……只是当时时机不太合适。那是非常忙碌的两天。”

特朗普还声称，他随时可以通过重启他们在其第一个任期内保持的信件往来来恢复与金正恩的外交，尽管他承认两位领导人“最近”没有通信。

金正恩此前曾表示，如果美国放弃对朝鲜的“敌对政策”并尊重他所称的朝鲜核国家地位，他就可以重返谈判。专家表示，金正恩旨在赢得国际社会对其核国家地位的承认，以便要求解除国际制裁。

上周，国际原子能机构总干事拉斐尔·格罗西评估称，朝鲜一直在扩建其位于宁边的原有铀浓缩设施，称此举“令人严重关切”。

核武器可以用高浓缩铀或武器级钚制造，朝鲜在宁边拥有生产这两种材料的设施。去年，韩国统一部长官郑东泳表示，朝鲜运营着四个铀浓缩设施，且每天都在运行。

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

Workers inflate the Spider-Man balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 on November 25, 2026 in New York City. Macy's plans to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables, but forecasted high winds are threatening to ground the giant balloons.

Adam Gray/Getty Images

hide caption

Adam Gray/Getty Images

• 🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.

• 🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. A German boat dealer is suspected of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

items.body:
Global Health

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

November 25, 20269:14 AM ET

Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption

Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

“我是倒数第二个——我排第十一，”她说。“利比里亚的家庭都很大。”

每年11月的第一个星期四，维亚的家人都会聚集在她成长的考德威尔镇，庆祝利比里亚感恩节。

“我们聚在一起时，队伍变得[太]庞大，你没法围坐在餐桌旁，”她解释道。“所以我们就在外面的树下聚会。我们相聚时，几乎就像在开派对。”

这个利比里亚节日可追溯到19世纪上半叶，当时美国殖民协会建立了后来发展成这个国家的社区。它由美国黑人创立——既有生来自由的黑人，也有被解放的奴隶——他们的离开有时是自愿的，有时是被迫的。“来自美国的定居者把那个感恩节传统带到了利比里亚，”维亚说。这一节日移植过来后，随着时间推移，因应国家事件而不断演变。

利比里亚于1847年获得独立，但英国继续试图夺取大片领土。1883年，身为圣公会牧师的总统阿尔弗雷德·弗朗西斯·拉塞尔祈求上帝帮助阻止入侵。

那次祈祷是“祈求保护、抵御入侵者，防止他们侵入我们的领土，”维亚说。

利比里亚人成功维护了主权。那一年，立法机构正式将感恩节确立为全国性节日，浸透着当时宗教性的感恩之情。

对所有人都是神圣的日子

维亚这样概括利比里亚感恩节：“这是感谢上帝赐予我们自由、赐予神圣庇护。这是感谢上帝赐予团结和丰收。”

维亚说，她家的庆祝活动与利比里亚许多家庭一样，从早上去教堂开始。但这个节日属于所有信仰的人，其他宗教群体也会纪念这个日子。

“穆斯林去清真寺祈祷，”塞库·穆罕默德·谢里夫说。他是一位YouTuber，走遍家乡利比里亚，展示当地的风物和文化遗产，包括感恩节。“穆斯林、基督徒和其他人——所有人都把这一天当作节日来庆祝。”

谢里夫小时候，这一天是他指望能添置新衣的日子。

“我爸爸过去会给我做的是，”谢里夫说，买一套“衬衫长裤套装，然后他会给我买拖鞋。”他最喜欢的套装是白色的。

多年来在感恩节，他渐渐习惯了吃各种炖菜，包括一种用红薯叶做的，还有一种用从园子里收集的蜗牛做的。

“我们叫它国王的肉，”谢里夫笑着说。“非常非常好吃。”

在利比里亚，下午三四点的那顿正餐各家不同。

伊冯娜·卡普哈特·维亚的侄女和侄子们在考德威尔的一次家庭聚会上盛满自己的盘子。

丽贝卡·布拉波·维亚

隐藏图注

丽贝卡·布拉波·维亚

“我们不吃火鸡，”维亚说，“但我们吃鸡。我们做炸鸡、熏鸡、烤鸡。”

维亚家还供应乔洛夫米饭、西瓜、菠萝和各种炖菜，包括一种叫富富配汤的。它是木薯、鱼、鸡、秋葵、辣椒等的混合。“这让汤非常美味，”维亚说。“每顿感恩节都[必须]有。”

（不过维亚并不特别喜欢做饭。“如果你对我说，‘去厨房做饭，还是坐在客厅看书，’”她说，“我会坐在客厅看书。”）

“我感谢上帝”

今年，谢里夫没有资源操办感恩节。但他说，他仍然感谢上帝让他保持健康，让利比里亚在1989年至1997年以及1999年至2003年的内战撕裂国家之后保持和平。

维亚也心怀感激。“我去过感恩节时，”她说，“我感谢上帝我从哪里来、我现在在哪里，我也感谢祂将带我去哪里，因为我知道祂掌管未来。”

维亚是We-Care基金会的项目经理，这是一家教育非营利组织，除其他工作外，还教儿童识字。“爱读书的孩子会成为爱读书的长者，”她说。

“我们期望知情的成年人做出知情的决定，影响他们的社会和经济生活”——或许，以他们有一天会心怀感激的方式。

Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.

• Transcript

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa.

Scott Olson/Getty Images

hide caption

Scott Olson/Getty Images

• 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

• 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

• 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.

Today's listen

Tatyana Alanis for NPR

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.

There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

Life advice

Beck Harlan for NPR

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

• 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

• 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.

• 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.

• 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.

For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

Ezra Frech of Team United States competes during the Men's Long Jump T63 Final on three of the World Para Athletics Championships New Delhi 2025 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on Sept. 29, 2025 in New Delhi, India.

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

hide caption

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

1. Dancing with the Stars wrapped up Season 35 last night, crowning Paralympian Ezra Frech and his partner, Daniella Karagach, as the winners of this year's Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

2. Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time.

3. Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.
